idiom_name: by-delegation over the new implementation + JVM signature annotations
implementation_notes: Kotlin absorbs the structural half of the window: the by-clause in a supertype list makes the compiler generate every forwarding member of the frozen interface, so the class costs one line and only the mapping and the calls needing argument juggling are written by hand - the delegation documentation states the pattern is supported natively, requiring zero boilerplate. On the JVM the emitted signature is the legacy shape for old Java callers, so @JvmName, @JvmOverloads and default arguments must be chosen deliberately rather than refactored casually. The hand-written form is still justified when the legacy contract is a class instead of an interface (delegation only forwards interface members) or when each method needs bespoke conversion.
pitfalls: @JvmName, @JvmOverloads and default arguments change the emitted JVM signatures: renaming a Kotlin member or dropping a default breaks Java callers while Kotlin code still compiles.
Delegation forwards neither equals/hashCode/toString nor members of a legacy class, and old clients may depend on both.
Kotlin's check/require/error helpers throw richer exception types than the old Java contract declared; catch and map them at the boundary.
